components.note: 口 (mouth) — words spoken by a mouth are what reach the ear, giving 听 its meaning 'to listen.'
斤 stands in for the ear in this simplified character — the target that spoken words reach.
至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.pinyin: Wǒ tīngdào yǒu rén zài qiāo mén.
example.english: I heard someone knocking on the door.
example.fact: 到 acts as a resultative complement meaning "successfully reaching a target" — 听到 literally means "listen and successfully arrive at [the sound]," i.e. actually hearing it, in contrast to the plain verb 听 ("to listen"), which just describes the act without confirming anything registered. The same 到-as-"successfully" pattern shows up in 看到 ("to see," lit. "look and reach") and 找到 ("to find," lit. "search and reach").

components.note: 毛 (fur, hair) — 表 originally pictured a fur garment worn on the outside.
衣 (clothing) — an outer fur wrap gave 表 its meaning of 'outer' or 'surface,' and later, 'to express' (showing something on the surface).
氵 (water) — 演 originally described water flowing and spreading out, later extended to 'developing, unfolding'
寅 (yín) gives a sound distantly related to 演's reading yǎn, having drifted apart over time

example.hanzi: 孩子们在台上表演节目。
example.pinyin: Háizimen zài tái shàng biǎoyǎn jiémù.
example.english: The children are performing on stage.
example.fact: 表演 covers both scripted, rehearsed performance (a play, a dance routine, a magic show) and, by extension, "putting on an act" insincerely in everyday speech (别表演了, "stop putting on a show") — the same slide from "staged performance" to "fake behavior" that English "act" undergoes.

meanings: to be in the process of

components.note: 一 (a line, representing a target or standard) — 正 shows a foot arriving exactly at the right mark.
止 (foot, to stop) — arriving and stopping precisely at the target gives 正 its meaning of 'correct' or 'straight.'
土 (earth/soil) — 在 originally related to standing on the ground
才 (cái) gives the sound — 在 is pronounced zài, a close match

example.pinyin: Tā zhèngzài xiě zuòyè.
example.english: He is in the middle of doing his homework.
example.fact: 正在 is one of Mandarin’s clearest markers of the progressive aspect ("right now, in the middle of") and sits directly before the verb — it is often reinforced by the sentence-final particle 呢 (他正在写作业呢), but unlike English "-ing," it can be dropped entirely once context already makes an ongoing action obvious.

components.note: 咸 (all, together) — 感 relates to a shared reaction.
心 (heart) — feelings that stir the heart gave 感 its meaning 'to feel' or 'emotion.'
至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.hanzi: 听到这个消息,我感到很惊讶。
example.pinyin: Tīngdào zhège xiāoxi, wǒ gǎndào hěn jīngyà.
example.english: Hearing this news, I felt very surprised.
example.fact: 感到 almost always introduces an emotional or sensory state via a following adjective or clause (感到惊讶, 感到高兴) and reads noticeably more formal than the everyday 觉得 — in casual speech 觉得 dominates, while 感到 shows up more in narration, news reports, and writing.

components.note: 辶 (walking/movement) — links 边's meaning to a boundary or edge one moves along.
臱 (biān) gives the sound — 边 is also pronounced biān, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ yǐzi fàng dào nàbian.
example.english: Please put the chair over there.
example.fact: 那边 pairs with 这边 ("over here") as Mandarin’s directional near/far duo built on location rather than a demonstrative pronoun — where 那里/这里 point at a place as a noun ("that place"), 那边/这边 point at a side or direction, often used together with a pointing gesture.

components.note: 攵 (an action) — ties to 故's sense of a cause or reason behind an action
古 (gǔ) gives a sound close to 故's reading gù

example.hanzi: 妈妈每天晚上给我讲一个故事。
example.pinyin: Māma měitiān wǎnshang gěi wǒ jiǎng yí gè gùshi.
example.english: Mom tells me a story every night.
example.fact: The everyday sense "story, tale" is read with a neutral tone on 事 (gùshi). Dictionaries also list the same two characters read with a full fourth tone, gùshì, for a separate, much rarer classical/literary sense, "a precedent, an old practice" — it is the common neutral-tone reading, not the toned classical one, that accounts for this word’s high frequency here.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 结 relates to tying or knotting threads together.
吉 (jí) gives a hint of the sound — 结 is pronounced jié, a connection that has shifted over time.
女 (woman) — 婚 relates to marriage, historically centered on the wife.
昏 (hūn) gives the sound — an exact match with 婚.

example.pinyin: Tāmen dǎsuàn míngnián jiéhūn.
example.english: They plan to get married next year.
example.fact: 结婚 is a verb-object compound (结 "to tie" + 婚 "marriage") that cannot take a person directly as its object — "to marry someone" has to be phrased with 跟/和 + person + 结婚 (我跟她结婚, never 我结婚她), a common structural trap for English speakers used to "marry" taking a direct object.

meanings: (dialect) (in a coaxing or familiar way) you

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 咱 is a spoken pronoun, used in speech.
自 (zì) shares the initial z- with zán, though the rhyme has drifted.
亻 (person) — 们 attaches to pronouns and nouns referring to people to mark plural, e.g. 我们 ('we'), 你们 ('you all')
门 (mén) gives a sound close to 们's reading (men)

example.pinyin: Zánmen yìqǐ qù chīfàn ba.
example.english: Let’s go eat together (you and I both).
example.fact: 咱们 is a northern-Mandarin variant of 我们 that many speakers still keep a distinction for: 咱们 is strictly inclusive, guaranteed to include the listener ("we, you and I"), while 我们 is ambiguous and can exclude the person being spoken to — a distinction English "we" doesn’t make at all.

meanings: to treat sth by a special process

components.note: 夂 (a foot, to go) — 处 relates to arriving somewhere.
卜 (a mark or flag) — planting a marker after arriving gave 处 its meaning of 'a place' or 'to settle, deal with.'
王 (a variant form of 玉, meaning jade) — 理 originally referred to the natural grain or pattern in jade, later extending to 'reason, logic, to manage.'
里 (lǐ) gives the sound — 理 is also pronounced lǐ, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì wǒ huì jǐnkuài chǔlǐ.
example.english: I will handle this matter as soon as possible.
example.fact: 处理 is the neutral, businesslike verb for handling a problem, task, or file — used everywhere from customer service (处理投诉, "handle complaints") to computing (数据处理, "data processing") — sitting a register above the casual 办 ("to do, handle") and below the heavier 解决 (also in this batch), which implies actually resolving something rather than just attending to it.

components.note: 女 (woman) sits at the base of the character.
彐-shaped strokes above picture a hand holding a broom, an old image of a wife managing the household.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.pinyin: Tā de qīzi shì yì míng yīshēng.
example.english: His wife is a doctor.
example.fact: With a neutral tone on 子, qīzi is the everyday word for "wife." The same two characters read with a full third tone, qīzǐ, name a separate, more literary sense, "wife and children" — the ordinary neutral-tone reading, not the toned literary one, is what makes 妻子 this common.

meanings: (of an army etc) to be on the march

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 进 relates to advancing or entering, both movement-related.
井 (jǐng) gives a close sound cue — 进 is pronounced jìn, sharing similar consonant and vowel sounds.
彳 depicts a step with the left foot; together with 亍 (a step with the right foot), 行 shows a person walking or moving.
亍 depicts a step with the right foot, complementing 彳 to form the idea of walking or travel.

example.pinyin: Huìyì zhèngzài jìnxíng.
example.english: The meeting is currently underway.
example.fact: 进行 is a formal, often bureaucratic-sounding verb that turns almost any action noun into a full verb phrase (进行调查 "carry out an investigation," 进行讨论 "hold a discussion") — a productive pattern common in news and official writing that lets a two-character noun stand in for a verb English would express more simply, like "investigate" or "discuss."

components.note: Traditionally analyzed as 日 combined with 疋, linked to the idea of speaking directly and truthfully — the source of 是's meaning 'to be, indeed, right.'
不 (not) — 否 relates directly to negation and denial
口 (kǒu) gives a loose sound connection to 否's reading fǒu

example.pinyin: Wǒ bù zhīdào tā shìfǒu huì lái.
example.english: I don’t know whether he will come.
example.fact: 是否 is the formal, written-register equivalent of the everyday spoken 是不是 or the simpler "V不V" pattern — reach for 是否 in a report or essay, and for 是不是 in conversation; using 是否 in casual chat can sound stiff, and 是不是 in a formal document can sound too colloquial.

components.note: 刂 (a knife, related to 刀) — ties to 刚's meaning 'firm, hard, strong'
冈 (gāng) gives the sound — 刚 is also pronounced gāng, an exact match
刂 (a knife, related to 刀) — ties to 刚's meaning 'firm, hard, strong'
冈 (gāng) gives the sound — 刚 is also pronounced gāng, an exact match

example.pinyin: Tā gānggang líkāi.
example.english: He just left.
example.fact: 刚刚 is 刚 ("just, a moment ago") reduplicated for emphasis, the same doubling device behind 谢谢 (seen in the pilot batch) — the doubled form sharpens the sense of recency compared to the plain, slightly less emphatic 刚 alone.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 案 originally referred to a wooden table or desk
安 (ān) gives a sound close to 案's reading àn, differing only in tone
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 警察还在调查这个案子。
example.pinyin: Jǐngchá hái zài diàochá zhège ànzi.
example.english: The police are still investigating this case.
example.fact: 案 by itself already meant a low wooden table or desk in antiquity, the kind an official might set documents on while reviewing a dispute — a traditional explanation for how 案子/案件 came to mean "a (legal) case" in modern usage, an object-turned-abstraction not unlike English "the case is on my desk."

components.note: 彳 depicts a step with the left foot; together with 亍 (a step with the right foot), 行 shows a person walking or moving.
亍 depicts a step with the right foot, complementing 彳 to form the idea of walking or travel.
力 (strength/force) — 动 relates to movement produced by exertion or force.

example.hanzi: 我们必须马上采取行动。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen bìxū mǎshàng cǎiqǔ xíngdòng.
example.english: We must take action immediately.
example.fact: 行动 most often appears as the object of the fixed verb 采取 ("采取行动," "to take action") rather than standing alone as a verb in everyday speech — one of many two-character nouns in Mandarin that habitually pair with one specific "light verb" rather than combining freely with any verb of doing.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — ancient texts were written on bound bamboo strips, and 第 originally referred to the sequential order of such strips, giving rise to its meaning 'ordinal number' (as in 第一, first).
二 is simply two horizontal strokes stacked together — the most direct way to picture the number two, following the same pattern as 一 (one) and 三 (three).

example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ dì èr cì lái Běijīng.
example.english: This is the second time I’ve come to Beijing.
example.fact: 第 is a dedicated ordinal-number prefix with no meaning of its own outside this role — attach it to any cardinal number (第一, 第二, 第三...) to turn "one, two, three" into "first, second, third," a far more regular system than English’s mix of "-th" endings and irregular forms like "first" and "second."

components.note: 力 (strength) — 努 relates to exerting effort and strength.
奴 (nú) gives a sound close to nǔ, sharing the same syllable body and differing only in tone.
力 depicts the blade of a plow — since plowing fields took great physical effort, the shape came to represent strength or power.

example.hanzi: 你只要努力,就一定能成功。
example.pinyin: Nǐ zhǐyào nǔlì, jiù yídìng néng chénggōng.
example.english: As long as you try hard, you’ll definitely succeed.
example.fact: 努力 functions equally well as a verb ("to work hard"), an adverb modifying another verb (努力学习, "study hard"), and an adjective describing a person (他很努力, "he’s hard-working") — one Mandarin word doing the job of three different English parts of speech.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 怕 relates to a feeling of fear in one's heart
白 (bái) gives a loose sound connection to 怕's reading pà

example.pinyin: Xiǎo háizi hěn hàipà dǎléi.
example.english: Small children are very afraid of thunder.
example.fact: 害怕 takes its feared object directly, as if it were an ordinary transitive verb (害怕打雷, "afraid of thunder"; 害怕黑暗, "afraid of the dark") — where English inserts "of" between the adjective "afraid" and its object, Chinese just runs the two together with no preposition needed.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — relates to 调's meaning 'to adjust, transfer,' something coordinated through spoken negotiation.
周 (zhōu) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from diào.

example.hanzi: 警方正在调查这起事故的原因。
example.pinyin: Jǐngfāng zhèngzài diàochá zhè qǐ shìgù de yuányīn.
example.english: The police are investigating the cause of this accident.
example.fact: 调查 covers everything from a formal police or journalistic investigation to a casual opinion poll (民意调查, "public opinion survey") — English splits this range across several words ("investigation," "inquiry," "survey," "poll"), while Chinese keeps one verb for the whole family of "systematically finding things out."

components.note: 丿 (something falling) — an object slipping away.
夫 (a hand/person) — the object slipping out of a hand, giving 失 its meaning 'to lose.'

example.hanzi: 他失去了一个很好的机会。
example.pinyin: Tā shīqù le yí gè hěn hǎo de jīhuì.
example.english: He lost a really good opportunity.
example.fact: 失去 is reserved for losing something abstract or irreplaceable — a chance, someone’s trust, a limb, a loved one — while the everyday verb for misplacing a physical object, like keys or an umbrella, is 丢 (丢钥匙, "lose one’s keys") — a distinction with no single equivalent in English "to lose."

components.note: 力 (strength/effort) — the exertion behind the achievement.
工 (work/labor) — results produced through skillful labor, giving 功 its meaning 'achievement, merit, skill.'

example.hanzi: 经过多次尝试,他终于成功了。
example.pinyin: Jīngguò duō cì chángshì, tā zhōngyú chénggōng le.
example.english: After many attempts, he finally succeeded.
example.fact: 成功 doubles as a stative verb ("to succeed," 成功了) and an adjective meaning "successful" (一个成功的人, "a successful person") without changing form — one more example, alongside 工作 in the pilot batch, of a Chinese word crossing freely between verb and adjective roles that English keeps grammatically separate ("succeed" vs. "successful").

components.note: 耂 (a variant of 老, 'old') — 考 relates to careful examination and testing
丂 gives a loose sound connection to 考's reading kǎo
虍 depicts a tiger's head or stripes.
心 (heart) — a heart facing a tiger's threat gave 虑 its meaning 'to worry, to be concerned.'

example.hanzi: 我需要考虑一下再决定。
example.pinyin: Wǒ xūyào kǎolǜ yíxià zài juédìng.
example.english: I need to think it over before deciding.
example.fact: 考虑 is built from 考 ("to examine, test") and 虑 ("to worry, deliberate") — two characters that separately name "scrutinizing" and "turning something over anxiously in the mind," compounding into the even-handed modern sense "to consider, think over."

meanings: just now (variant of 剛才|刚才[gang1 cai2])

components.note: 刂 (a knife, related to 刀) — ties to 刚's meaning 'firm, hard, strong'
冈 (gāng) gives the sound — 刚 is also pronounced gāng, an exact match
才 depicts a young sprout just breaking through the soil — new growth came to represent budding talent or ability.

example.pinyin: Gāngcái shì shéi zài qiāo mén?
example.english: Who was knocking on the door just now?
example.fact: 刚才 and its near-twin 刚刚 (also in this batch) both mean "just now," but 刚才 usually points to a slightly looser stretch of recent time — anywhere from moments to an hour ago — and can stand alone as an answer to "when," while 刚刚 emphasizes the very instant something happened and almost always attaches directly to the verb it modifies.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 约 originally meant 'to bind, tie up,' extending to 'to agree, arrange' and 'approximately.'
人 (people) over 云 (clouds/say) — a picture of people gathering and speaking together, related to 会's meanings 'to meet' and 'to know how to.'

example.pinyin: Wǒmen jīnwǎn yǒu yí gè yuēhuì.
example.english: We have a date tonight.
example.fact: 约会 covers both a romantic "date" and a plain scheduled "appointment," a broader range than English keeps in one word — context alone, such as talking about a doctor’s office versus talking about a crush, tells a listener which sense is meant.

components.note: 节 is the simplified form of 節, which depicted the segmented sections of a bamboo stalk ⺮ — giving 节 its meaning 'joint, section, festival.'
目 depicts an eye turned on its side, with the outline and pupil visible — later straightened into today's rectangular shape.

example.hanzi: 你最喜欢哪个电视节目?
example.pinyin: Nǐ zuì xǐhuan nǎge diànshì jiémù?
example.english: Which TV show do you like best?
example.fact: 目 by itself is a pictograph of an eye — in 节目, that "eye" sits beside 节 (originally a bamboo joint, later "a division, a section"), giving the compound its literal sense of a discrete segment set before an audience’s eyes, and its modern meaning "program, show."

components.note: 辶 (to walk, movement) — 通 relates to passing through or getting somewhere.
甬 (yǒng) gives a hint of the sound — 通 is pronounced tōng, a connection that has shifted over time.
辶 (to walk/move) — shows 过's core meaning of 'passing through' or 'crossing'
咼 (guō) gives a sound close to 过's reading guò; the simplified form 过 now uses 寸 in place of 咼, but the phonetic connection traces back to the traditional character 過

example.pinyin: Tā tōngguò le zhè cì kǎoshì.
example.english: He passed this exam.
example.fact: 通过 slides between three related jobs in one word: a verb meaning "to pass" (通过考试, "pass an exam"), a verb meaning "to approve, adopt" (通过决议, "pass a resolution"), and a preposition meaning "by means of, via" (通过努力, "through hard work") — context, not form, tells a listener which one is in play.

components.note: A stylized foot (related to 止, 'to stop/foot') — originally meant 'to go,' later grammaticalized into a literary possessive/linking particle, similar to 的.
门 (door/gate) — 间 pictures light passing through an entryway.
日 (sun) — sunlight shining through a gap in a doorway gave 间 its meaning of a space 'in between,' as in 中间 (in the middle) or 时间 (time, the space between moments).

example.hanzi: 中国和日本之间隔着一片大海。
example.pinyin: Zhōngguó hé Rìběn zhījiān gézhe yí piàn dà hǎi.
example.english: A great expanse of sea lies between China and Japan.
example.fact: 之 is a literary, almost fossilized possessive particle — its everyday equivalent is the far more common 的 — but 之间 (like 之前 "before" and 之后 "after") keeps this old-fashioned 之 alive as a fixed set phrase rather than as a rule a learner can extend freely.

components.note: 另 (other, separate) — 别 relates to distinguishing one thing from another.
刂 (knife) — cutting things apart to sort them gave 别 its meaning 'to separate' or 'other,' and later, 'don't' as a command.

example.pinyin: Nǐ hái xūyào biéde dōngxi ma?
example.english: Do you need anything else?
example.fact: 别的 is the everyday, spoken-register word for "other, else" (别的东西, 别的人), while its near-synonym 其他 reads a shade more formal and shows up more often in writing and set expressions (其他人, 其他情况) — close enough in meaning that a learner can usually swap one for the other without changing what a sentence means, just its register.

components.note: 廾 (two hands) — depicts hands at work.
一 represents the latch or bar of a door; hands lifting it away gave 开 its meaning 'to open, to start.'
心 was originally a pictograph of the physical shape of a human heart, and came to represent the mind, feelings, and intention as well.

example.pinyin: Jīntiān wánr de hěn kāixīn.
example.english: Today was a lot of fun.
example.fact: 开心 pictures happiness almost literally — 开 ("to open") plus 心 ("heart"), "an opened-up heart" — a transparent compositional image sitting right alongside its near-synonym 高兴, the more neutral, general-purpose word for "happy" in everyday Mandarin.

components.note: 母 depicts a kneeling woman with two dots marking breasts — an image emphasizing nursing and motherhood, giving 母 its meaning 'mother.'
木 (tree) — traditionally read as a tree that has borne fruit.
立 (standing) — standing close by to watch it grow, evoking closeness and nurture, extended to 亲's meaning 'close, dear; parent, relative.'

example.pinyin: Mǔqīn jié kuàilè!
example.english: Happy Mother’s Day!
example.fact: 母亲 is the formal, written-register word for "mother," reserved for essays, official contexts, and set phrases like 母亲节 ("Mother’s Day") — in daily conversation Chinese speakers overwhelmingly say 妈妈 instead, much like English speakers default to "mom" over the more formal "mother" in casual speech.

components.note: 丶 (a dot) — represents the burning flame atop a lamp.
王 here depicts the base and stand of an oil lamp, not its usual meaning 'king' — the one who tends the flame became linked to 'master, lord, main.'
心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.

example.hanzi: 我们再想想别的主意吧。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen zài xiǎngxiang biéde zhǔyi ba.
example.english: Let’s think of some other ideas.
example.fact: 主意 names a practical plan or decision one settles on (拿主意, "make up one’s mind"; 出主意, "suggest an idea/plan") rather than an abstract thought or concept, which is instead 想法 or 观念 — 主意 is the "idea" you act on, not the "idea" you merely have.

components.note: 大 (a grown man) — the figure being depicted.
一 (a hairpin) — worn across the top of the head to mark a coming-of-age ceremony, giving 夫 its meaning 'man, husband.'

example.pinyin: Tā de zhàngfu zài guówài gōngzuò.
example.english: Her husband works abroad.
example.fact: 丈 doubles as a unit of length (about 3.3 meters) and, in older usage, a mark of seniority or full adulthood — the same 丈 shows up in 丈人 ("father-in-law") and 老丈 ("old man"). 丈夫, traditionally glossed as "a person of full-grown stature," narrowed over time from a general term for a grown man to today’s specific meaning, "husband."

example.hanzi: 毛毛虫最后变成了蝴蝶。
example.pinyin: Máomaochóng zuìhòu biànchéng le húdié.
example.english: The caterpillar eventually turned into a butterfly.
example.fact: 成 works here as a resultative complement meaning "into a completed new state" — 变成 literally "change into," in contrast to the bare verb 变 ("to change"), which only says something is changing without specifying what it changes into.

components.note: 角 (horn) — 解 pictures removing a part of an animal.
牛 (ox) — together with a knife cutting between horn and ox, 解 pictures separating something into parts, giving its meaning 'to untie' or 'to explain.'
釆 (to distinguish/sort) — 释 relates to sorting out and clarifying, i.e. 'to explain'
睪 (yì) gives a sound distantly related to 释's reading shì, having drifted apart over time

example.hanzi: 请你解释一下这个词的意思。
example.pinyin: Qǐng nǐ jiěshì yíxià zhège cí de yìsi.
example.english: Please explain the meaning of this word.
example.fact: 解 alone already carries the sense "to untie, to loosen" (as in 解开, "to undo a knot"), and 解释 extends that image figuratively — "untying" a confusing idea into something clear — the same root 解 that appears in 解决 (also in this batch), Mandarin’s verb for "resolving" a problem.

meanings: variant of 聯繫|联系[lian2 xi4]

components.note: 耳 (ear) — 联 originally meant 'connected, linked,' perhaps through the image of joined loops.
关 (guān) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from lián.
糸 (thread/silk) — 系 relates to connecting or tying things together, like threads linking into a system.

example.pinyin: Yǒushì qǐng suíshí liánxì wǒ.
example.english: If anything comes up, please contact me anytime.
example.fact: 联系 works equally well as a verb ("to get in touch with someone," 联系我) and a noun ("a connection, a relationship," 保持联系, "keep in touch") with no change in form — common enough in Mandarin that it’s worth checking both the verb and noun gloss whenever a new two-character word like this shows up.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — the act of speaking.
正 (straight, correct) — speaking the straight, correct truth, giving 证 its meaning 'to prove, certify; evidence.'
日 (sun) — combined with 月 (moon), 明 shows the light of both sun and moon, giving the meaning 'bright' or 'clear.'
月 (moon) — together with 日 (sun), the two brightest things in the sky represent brightness and clarity.

example.hanzi: 这张照片可以证明他当时在场。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhāng zhàopiàn kěyǐ zhèngmíng tā dāngshí zàichǎng.
example.english: This photo can prove that he was present at the time.
example.fact: 证明 functions as both the verb "to prove" and the noun "a certificate, proof document" (身份证明, "identity certificate") — English keeps a similar verb/noun split ("to prove" vs. "proof"), but 证明 additionally covers the concrete bureaucratic sense of an official paper you must submit, with no single-word English equivalent.

meanings: life (as the characteristic of living beings)

components.note: 屮 (a young shoot) growing up out of 土 (earth/soil) — a picture of new life emerging from the ground.
令 (an order, command) — 命 pictures issuing a command.
口 (mouth) — a command given aloud gave 命 its meaning 'order' or 'decree,' and by extension, 'fate' or 'life.'

example.hanzi: 每一个生命都值得尊重。
example.pinyin: Měi yí gè shēngmìng dōu zhídé zūnzhòng.
example.english: Every life deserves respect.
example.fact: 生命 names life as a biological or philosophical force — "life" in the abstract, as something precious or at risk — while the similar-looking 生活 means "life" in the sense of daily living and lifestyle; mixing the two up is a common learner slip since English "life" covers both.

components.note: 月 (yuè) here actually derives from 肉 (meat) — 有 originally depicted a hand holding meat, meaning 'to possess'; it also lends a loose phonetic connection to yǒu.
灬 (fire) — 点 originally related to a small flame or dot of light, giving rise to the meaning 'dot' or 'point.'
占 (zhàn) gives a hint of the sound — 点 is pronounced diǎn, a connection that has drifted over the centuries.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jīntiān yǒudiǎn lèi.
example.english: I’m a little tired today.
example.fact: 有点 sits directly before an adjective to soften it (有点累, "a bit tired"; 有点贵, "a bit pricey") and tends to modify something negative or undesirable far more often than something positive — native speakers reach for 有点丑 ("a bit ugly") much more readily than 有点好看 ("a bit good-looking"), an asymmetry that trips up learners who treat 有点 as a neutral intensifier.

components.note: 角 (horn) — 解 pictures removing a part of an animal.
牛 (ox) — together with a knife cutting between horn and ox, 解 pictures separating something into parts, giving its meaning 'to untie' or 'to explain.'

example.pinyin: Zhège wèntí hěn nán jiějué.
example.english: This problem is very hard to solve.
example.fact: 解决 implies actually resolving a problem down to nothing left to deal with, in contrast to 处理 (also in this batch), which just means attending to or handling something — you can 处理 a complaint without truly 解决-ing the underlying issue, a distinction useful for calibrating how thoroughly something was dealt with.

components.note: 力 (strength) — relates to 办's meaning 'to handle, manage, do,' something accomplished through effort.
八 (bā) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from bàn.
八 here depicts something splitting apart or being divided.
厶 is an old form meaning 'private' or 'one's own' — 公 shows dividing up private property to share it fairly, giving rise to the meaning 'public' or 'fair.'
宀 (roof) — 室 refers to an enclosed room under a roof
至 (zhì) gives the sound — an exact match with 室's reading shì

example.pinyin: Wǒ de bàngōngshì zài sān lóu.
example.english: My office is on the third floor.
example.fact: 办公室 is built from three transparent pieces stacked together — 办 ("to handle, do"), 公 ("public, official"), and 室 ("room") — literally "a room for handling official business," a [verb][domain][place-noun] pattern many three-character Mandarin nouns follow.

components.note: 又 (a hand) — reaching out to try to catch something.
隹 (a bird) — catching a bird by hand is hard, giving 难 its meaning 'difficult.'
辶 (to walk) — 道 relates to a path or road one walks along.
首 (shǒu) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer resembles dào, a reminder that sound components can drift after thousands of years of pronunciation change.

example.hanzi: 难道你忘了今天是我的生日?
example.pinyin: Nándào nǐ wàng le jīntiān shì wǒ de shēngrì?
example.english: Don’t tell me you forgot today is my birthday?
example.fact: 难道 doesn’t ask a real question — it’s a rhetorical marker that frames the speaker’s surprise or disbelief, expecting the listener to confirm what the speaker already suspects, closer in function to English "don’t tell me..." or "surely..." than to a genuine yes/no question word like 吗.

components.note: 亻 (person) plus 乍 (suddenly/for the first time) — together suggesting a person making or doing something for the first time.

example.hanzi: 作为一名老师,她非常有耐心。
example.pinyin: Zuòwéi yì míng lǎoshī, tā fēicháng yǒu nàixīn.
example.english: As a teacher, she is very patient.
example.fact: 作为 at the head of a phrase means "in the capacity of, as" (作为学生, "as a student") — a role-framing device distinct from its other, noun-like sense, "one’s conduct, actions" (他的作为让人失望, "his conduct was disappointing"), two meanings sharing one written form but doing very different grammatical jobs.

components.note: 大 (a person, arms outstretched) — represents a rider.
可 here is said to depict a mount — a person riding in an unusual way gave 奇 its meaning 'strange, odd, remarkable.'

example.pinyin: Tā jīntiān de xíngwéi hěn qíguài.
example.english: His behavior today is very strange.
example.fact: 奇怪 doubles as a plain adjective ("strange, odd") and, in the first person, an expression of the speaker’s own puzzlement (我觉得奇怪, or simply 奇怪 said alone as an interjection, "how odd!") — much like English "strange" can be either a description or a muttered reaction.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 极 originally named the ridgepole, the highest beam of a roof, extended to 'extreme, utmost.'
及 (jí) gives the sound — 极 is also pronounced jí, an exact match.
Depicts a child wrapped in swaddling, related to 子 (child); the picture-meaning has nothing to do with its modern grammatical role marking a completed action or change of state.

example.pinyin: Zhège diànyǐng hǎokàn jí le.
example.english: This movie is extremely good.
example.fact: 极了 always follows the adjective it intensifies rather than preceding it (好看极了, never 极了好看) — the mirror image of English pre-adjective intensifiers like "extremely," and a word-order pattern shared by a small family of post-posed intensifiers including 得很 and 死了.

components.note: 凡 (common/ordinary) — suggests something shared or held in common.
口 (mouth) — sharing a common mouth/voice with others gave 同 its meaning of 'same, together.'
心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.

example.pinyin: Dàjiā dōu tóngyì zhège jìhuà.
example.english: Everyone agrees with this plan.
example.fact: 同 contributes "same, together" and 意 contributes "opinion, intention" — 同意 reads almost transparently as "sharing the same opinion," a compositional logic clear enough that a learner who already knows both characters separately can often guess the compound’s meaning on first encounter.

components.note: 氵 (water) — the sea or river being traveled through
斿 — a banner streaming in the wind, evoking free, drifting movement
又 (hand) shows a hand performing an action.
戈 (spear) — mock combat and stage tricks with weapons gave 戏 its meaning 'play, drama.'

example.pinyin: Wǒmen lái wán yí gè yóuxì ba.
example.english: Let’s play a game.
example.fact: 游戏 covers everything from a children’s playground game to a board game to a video game (电子游戏/网络游戏) — English needs the qualifier "video" or "computer" to narrow "game" down to the digital sense, while Chinese speakers usually just say 游戏 and let context supply which kind is meant.

components.note: 邦 (a nation/state) — a community bound together
巾 (a flag/cloth) — a banner people rally around to support one another
忄 (heart) — 忙 describes an inner state, here one of pressure or urgency.
亡 depicts loss or fleeing — paired with the heart, it suggests a mind under pressure, giving 忙 its meaning 'busy, rushed.'

example.hanzi: 你能帮忙拿一下这个箱子吗?
example.pinyin: Nǐ néng bāngmáng ná yíxià zhège xiāngzi ma?
example.english: Can you help carry this box?
example.fact: 帮忙 is a verb-object compound (帮 "to help" + 忙 "a task, a favor") that generally cannot take a person as its direct object — "help someone" needs 帮 alone with the person slotted in (帮我, "help me") since 帮忙他 is not standard, the same kind of built-in object restriction seen in 结婚 (also in this batch).

components.note: 厃 depicts a steep, overhanging cliff edge.
㔾 depicts a person crouching — together with 厃, the image of someone perched at a cliff's edge gave 危 its meaning 'dangerous.'
阝 (hill) — 险 originally referred to steep, dangerous terrain
佥 (qiān) gives a sound distantly related to 险's reading xiǎn, having drifted apart over time

example.pinyin: Xiǎoxīn, zhè tiáo lù hěn wēixiǎn.
example.english: Be careful, this road is very dangerous.
example.fact: 危 by itself is traditionally analyzed as a person crouched at the edge of a steep overhang — a vivid, almost literal image of precariousness that survives intact in the modern compound 危险, "danger."

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 讨 involves speaking, as in asking or discussing.
寸 (a hand/small measure) — combined with speech, suggests reaching out verbally to ask for something, giving 讨 its meaning 'to ask for, to discuss.'
厂 (a cliff shape) reflects 厌's original meaning related to a rock formation, later shifted to mean "to dislike."
犬 (quǎn) gives a sound distantly related to yàn, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Wǒ tǎoyàn xiàyǔ tiān.
example.english: I dislike rainy days.
example.fact: 讨厌 doubles as a verb ("to dislike, loathe") and an adjective describing an annoying person or thing (真讨厌!, "so annoying!") — in the adjective use it’s also commonly said fondly or teasingly among close friends and couples, similar to how English "you’re terrible" can be an affectionate jab rather than a real complaint.

meanings: (past tense marker used before verb or clause)

components.note: Originally pictured a container for steaming food: 日 at the bottom represents the heat or cooking vessel, and 丷 at the top shows the steam rising and escaping — giving 曾 its meaning 'once, already.'
纟 (silk/thread) — 经 originally referred to the vertical warp threads in weaving.
工 (gōng) gives a related sound cue for 经 (jīng), reflecting an older, closer pronunciation link between the two.

example.hanzi: 我曾经在北京住过三年。
example.pinyin: Wǒ céngjīng zài Běijīng zhù guo sān nián.
example.english: I once lived in Beijing for three years.
example.fact: 曾经 marks a past experience that no longer holds true now — it typically pairs with the experiential aspect particle 过 on the verb (住过, "have lived [there] at some point") rather than the completion particle 了, signaling that this happened once, but that chapter is now closed.
